mappings.note: the Rowlatt Act of February 1919 is the post-war repression LO-3 names as the trigger; C-1.1 because the cells asked for are a statute name and a date
Dandi was chosen as the launch point of Civil Disobedience, a choice of strategy (LO-2); C-1.1 because the item only asks the place to be named
both statements are about which urban groups joined -- Madras' Justice Party staying in, merchants refusing foreign trade -- which is LO-1's participation, not the design of the programme
Simon and Purna Swaraj are Congress strategy and outweigh the single LO-3 item (Rowlatt); C-1.1 because only the order is tested
a leader's portrait ringed with temple, mosque and church is nationalist iconography making one people out of many -- LO-1's collective belonging, not Tilak's strategy
the pair turns on telling Awadh's peasants (Baba Ramchandra) from the Gudem tribals (Raju) and on what the Kisan Sabha was for -- rural participation, LO-1
date-ordering across 1915-22 with two events in LO-3 (Jallianwala, Khilafat) and two in LO-2 (Gandhiji's return, Chauri Chaura); no single outcome is probed, the demand is chronology
why the town movement lost its participants (costly khadi, students drifting back) is about the urban social base, LO-1; the mill-output claim is only the distractor
the four steps are the Rowlatt-to-martial-law chain that LO-3 identifies as the trigger; C-1.1 because the item is an ordering of that chain
the Round Table Conferences are the negotiating arm of Congress strategy (LO-2); C-1.1 because the missing cells are a date and a statute
Vande Mataram and the Bharat Mata painting are the icons LO-1 covers; the test is attribution within that iconography, not any leader's method
the passage is about the First World War itself, and LO-3 is the only outcome in this frame that names the war; note the fit is to the war, not yet to its Indian effects
the 'Go back Simon' protest and its real cause (no Indian member) is Congress strategy in the run-up to Civil Disobedience; the Dandi March is the false reason, so LO-2 not LO-1

Raju's hold over the Gudem rebels is how a tribal community read the movement in its own terms -- a facet of belonging (LO-1); he was not a leader of a movement Gandhiji organised, so LO-2 does not reach him

asks the British motive for the Simon Commission; no outcome covers colonial constitutional policy in its own right, and the commission enters this chapter only through the Congress response, so LO-2 is the nearest
the strikes and attacks that followed Jallianwala Bagh are part of the post-war provocation LO-3 traces into Non-Cooperation
why a community stayed out of the united struggle is the limit of collective belonging -- LO-1; the Poona-Pact style leader negotiations would be LO-2
folklore revival is one of the cultural processes LO-1 names as ushering in collective belonging
the keyed answer defines Civil Disobedience by who took part ('people from all sections'), so LO-1; the question itself is too open to fix on the strategy reading
the withdrawal after Chauri Chaura is a decision about the method, the core of LO-2's 'effectiveness of the strategies'
same ground as item 42 -- a community's distance from the united struggle, LO-1; note the keyed answer dates the reason to Rehmat Ali in 1933, after the movement it explains
why the Congress kept workers' demands out is about which groups the movement did and did not absorb -- LO-1, not a judgement on Gandhian technique
temple-entry satyagrahas and persuading the upper castes are Gandhiji's own programme (LO-2); the dalits' own limited participation would be LO-1
why salt was picked is the design of the campaign -- LO-2's strategy; LO-1 would apply only if the question asked who then joined
begar, revenue and insecure tenure are the peasants' own grievances that pulled them in -- LO-1's facets of the movement, not Gandhiji's plan for it
